how-much-to-charge-to-build-a-sunroom.ht.text:
Sunroom bid calculator

How much to charge to build a sunroom

A published “$180 a square foot” special prices the floor. A residential sunroom is not a floor. It is glazed wall that does not scale with square feet, a thermal floor that may be an overlay or a new slab, an existing roof or a new insulated one, and often HVAC and a second slider. Matching the coupon on a 12×16 four-season room is how a sold job becomes a two-week loss after the first wall of glass.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a square-foot special cannot see

Take a 10×12 attached three-season on an existing deck, existing roof, vinyl windows, one slider. That is 32 lineal feet of wall and 256 square feet of glass — on a 120 square-foot floor. The coupon says $21,600. Raise the same shop to a 12×16 four-season. The floor is 192 square feet, so the coupon says $34,560. The glass did not scale that way: 40 lineal feet, insulated units, a new slab, an insulated roof, and often a mini-split the 10×12 never had.

Put four-season glass on that 12×16. Glass now costs more per square foot the vinyl 10×12 never priced. 10-foot walls are not “the same job plus two feet.” A second slider is not in the square-foot number at all.

How to price it

  1. Measure width along the house and depth out from the wall.
  2. Count glazed wall: three sides if attached, four if it wraps. Glass square feet is that perimeter times the glass height after the knee wall.
  3. Add window units at your widths, knee-wall lineal feet when the job is not full-height glass, and floor or roof on the whole footprint when you are actually building them.
  4. Price enclosure (three-season vinyl / four-season insulated), sliders, HVAC, electrical, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The sunroom bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting window widths, glass rates, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a catalog or a code table.

What this is not

This is not a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use. Hosted URLs, when they exist, may be taken offline without notice; there is no availability SLA.

Common questions

How much to charge to build a sunroom?

Start from the floor, count the glazed-wall square feet a square-foot special cannot see, then add the thermal floor, insulated roof, HVAC, electrical, and the permit. A published $180 per square foot special only sees width times depth.

Why do glass and a four-season enclosure change the price?

A 10-by-12 three-season on an existing deck is 32 lineal feet of wall and 256 square feet of vinyl glass on a 120 square-foot floor. A 12-by-16 four-season adds insulated glass, a new slab, an insulated roof, and often a mini-split. Matching the 10-by-12 coupon is how the four-season job loses money.

Is this a building-code calculation?

No. Window widths, spans, and glass rates here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not a building-code opinion, a permit, or an engineering stamp.

FOR SUNROOM, THREE-SEASON, AND FOUR-SEASON CREWS

Bid the glass, the floor, and the roof.

Price a residential sunroom the way the trade actually loses money: glazed-wall square feet a floor-square-foot special cannot see, then the thermal floor, the insulated roof, HVAC, extras, permit, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the job price, what it works out to per floor square foot, and the number below which the job loses money.

Looking up how much to charge to build a sunroom? Start here, then replace every starting figure with your own crew times.

A starting job

Pick a common call to fill the spans, enclosure, floor, and roof. Changing a kit never overwrites hours or material costs you have already typed.

The room

Width is along the house. Depth is the projection. An attached sunroom glazes three sides; a wrap glazes four. These are starting points, not a code opinion.

Hours and counts

Perimeter, glass, windows, knee wall, floor, and roof start from the geometry. Enclosure hours apply to the glazed wall. Change them when the site disagrees.

Materials and your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. A square-foot special written on the floor never sees it — or the glass.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the homeowner — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

The numbers ride after the #, which is never sent to a server, so copying a link uploads nothing. The customer should get the price, not the link.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting spans, window widths, hours, and material rates are common ballpark figures, not a building-code opinion, a permit, a warranty, or an engineering stamp. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why does the effective hourly rate read $639?

    Because it is a check figure, not a labor rate. The default room prices at $15,193.99 over 23.788 hours, but $8,269 of that is the kit, glazing, and finishes — against $1,175.13 of labor. Dividing the whole price by crew hours flatters the number on any material-heavy job. It is useful for spotting a job that has quietly become all-material-no-margin, not for setting a shop rate.

    Does $126.62 per square foot scale to a bigger room?

    Not reliably. It is $15,193.99 over the default 120 sq ft, and several of the biggest inputs — the mobilization, the tie-in to the existing structure, the permit, the site day — do not grow with floor area. A 240 sq ft room costs more than a 120 sq ft one but well short of double. Per-square-foot figures are for comparing two quotes on the same size room.

    What is not in this number?

    The things that most often turn a sunroom quote into a construction project: foundation or slab work, structural modification where the room ties into the house, HVAC extension, electrical circuits, and any engineering or drawings your jurisdiction requires for a permanent addition. A three-season room on an existing deck and a conditioned year-round addition price very differently, and only the first is close to the defaults here.

    Why is the margin a division rather than a markup?

    Because a 25% margin means profit is 25% of the price. The default room costs $11,395.50, so the price is $11,395.50 ÷ 0.75 = $15,193.99. Adding 25% to cost would give $14,244.37 and leave you at exactly a 20% margin — a $950 difference on one room, which is most of a week’s profit on a job this size.

vs-a-flat-180-per-square-foot-special.ht.text:
← Sunroom Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $180/sf special

“$180 a square foot” is not a price for a sunroom — it is a price for one specific enclosure, foundation, roof, and HVAC scope, quietly applied to every room that calls in.

What a flat $180/sf special is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote: multiply the room's footprint by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one room — a three-season enclosure on an existing deck, with the existing roof left alone, no HVAC, no electrical — and then reused for every room afterward, whether or not the next one looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the attachment style, enclosure (three-season or four-season), foundation (existing deck, existing slab, or new slab), roof (existing or new insulated), wall height, dimensions, windows, and sliders, plus whether the room needs HVAC, electrical, or a permit, and your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the glass, floor, roof, and mechanical scope separately by enclosure and foundation type, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this room, not a generic one.

What a flat $180/sf special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sf whether the enclosure is three-season vinyl or four-season insulated glass — even though four-season glass alone triples both the install hours per 100 sf and the material cost per foot. Prices glass hours and material by enclosure kit, so a four-season room is never quoted off a three-season rate.
Has no line for foundation work, regardless of whether the room lands on an existing deck overlay or needs a full new insulated slab poured. Prices floor hours and material by foundation kit — existing deck, existing slab, or new slab — so a new pour costs more than a finish pass on what is already there.
Has no line for an insulated roof, regardless of whether the existing roof is reused or a new one has to go on. Prices roof hours and material only when a new insulated roof is scoped, so leaving the existing roof alone never gets charged for one.
Has no line for HVAC, electrical, or a permit, regardless of how many the room needs. Prices HVAC hours and a mini-split fee, electrical hours and package cost, and a permit fee separately when scoped, so a fully mechanical room costs more than a shell.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat rate would have quoted the same room, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two rooms, the same footprint-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($38/hr crew wage, 30% burden, $140 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin):

RoomThis calculator's priceA flat $180/sf special, applied by footprint aloneGap
120 sq ft (10×12) three-season, existing deck, existing roof — the room the flat number is named for$15,194.00 bid price; $11,395.50 break-even cost$21,600.00The flat special runs $10,204.50 over this room's own break-even cost, and $6,406.00 over the calculator's own bid price — generous on the cheap end.
192 sq ft (12×16) four-season, new slab, insulated roof, HVAC and electrical$47,240.63 bid price; $35,430.47 break-even cost$34,560.00The same $180/sf special quotes $870.47 below this room's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $12,680.63 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the literal $180/sf rate named in the calculator's own worked presets, applied to each room's own footprint (120 sf and 192 sf). The same number that pads the three-season room's margin by more than half again turns into an outright loss the moment the enclosure, foundation, roof, and mechanicals change — even though a per-square-foot rate has no way to see any of that. Run your own room's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one room it was built for, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $180/sf special get a sunroom quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is enclosure type, foundation, roof, and HVAC, not floor area. A four-season room needs insulated glass, a new insulated slab instead of an existing deck overlay, an insulated roof instead of the existing one, and a mini-split -- none of which scale with the footprint the way a per-square-foot rate assumes. A flat $180/sf special charges all of that the same as the three-season room it was priced from.

What does a flat $180/sf special usually leave out entirely?

Foundation work, an insulated roof, and HVAC or electrical. A room built on an existing deck with the existing roof left alone is doing three fewer things than one with a new insulated slab, a new insulated roof, and a mini-split and electrical package added -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 120 sq ft three-season room on an existing deck and roof costs $11,395.50 to build. The flat $180/sf special charges $21,600.00 for that room -- $10,204.50 over cost, and even $6,406.00 above this calculator's own 25%-margin bid price. Applied to a 192 sq ft four-season room with a new slab, an insulated roof, and HVAC and electrical, the same $180/sf special charges $34,560.00 -- $870.47 below that room's own $35,430.47 cost to build, before a dollar of profit, and $12,680.63 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat $180/sf special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical rooms -- same enclosure type, same foundation, no new roof or HVAC either time -- a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own cheap-end preset it lands generous. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which room it was built on and neither does the estimator until the enclosure, foundation, roof, and HVAC scope are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the room's dimensions, enclosure type, foundation, roof, HVAC and electrical scope, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this room -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Sunroom Bid Calculator to price your own room, or read the pricing walkthrough.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs, and against a qualified professional and the authority having jurisdiction, before relying on it or submitting a bid. vs-jobber.html.text:
← Sunroom Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this sunroom build cost, given its glass, floor, and roof, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes glazed-wall square feet, thermal floor, insulated roof, and HVAC, plus loaded wage, material rates, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go — including the glass share of direct cost a floor-square-foot special cannot see — and a copyable customer-facing bid summary, plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Is the price I'm about to quote still above my walk-away cost for this job?This calculator's walk-away price check.
I need one shared account so my whole crew is scheduling, invoicing, and collecting payment the same way.Jobber, or a comparable field-service platform.
How does the math behind a sunroom bid actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Jobber is used through a subscription account.

Most sunroom and three-season crews get different value from each: Jobber (or a comparable field-service platform) for running client management, scheduling, invoicing, and payments across a whole business as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one sunroom build should cost from its glass, floor, and roof before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal, and neither this calculator nor Jobber is a code determination, a permit, or an engineering stamp for the structure or the glazing.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and a sunroom or three-season crew of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
